summary: Describes the Referral LDAP Service, an experimental service that uses LDAP and well-known LDAP types to make domain administrative data available. Such registration data had typically been exposed through Nicname/Whois. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Whois is an old phone book for who owns a web name. This tries using a different, more organized kind of directory to share the same kind of information.

questions: how does ldap serve domain registration data
what is the referral ldap service
why use ldap instead of whois
what problems did the ldap experiment find
subtitle: Using LDAP as a directory service for domain registration data.

tldr.problem: Domain registration data was traditionally exposed via Nicname/Whois, a text-based protocol that lacks structure, makes machine-reading difficult, and allows data mining. Registries needed a more controlled, structured way to distribute this information.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3663 describes the Referral LDAP Service, an experimental approach using LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) to organize domain administrative data into hierarchical Directory Information Trees (DITs), with referrals to direct clients between registry, registrar, and registrant servers.
tldr.outcome: The experiment demonstrated that LDAP could work for this purpose but revealed practical challenges with referrals, client implementations, and usability. This remains an Experimental protocol.

facts.label: Data expansion factor
facts.value: 20 million to 115 million entries without normalization

today: RFC 3663 remains Experimental. It describes a research project by VeriSign to explore LDAP as an alternative to Whois for domain registration data. While the experiment succeeded in demonstrating technical feasibility, it also revealed practical challenges that have prevented widespread adoption. Today, Whois and newer systems like RDAP (REST API for Domain Data, RFC 7480) remain the primary ways to access domain registration information.

sections.title: Background and Motivations
sections.content:
Domain registration information was originally meant to be served via X.500 directories, but due to implementation problems, a temporary Nicname/Whois server was set up instead. That temporary solution became permanent, and Whois is still used today, though it has limitations: the output is hard for machines to parse, anyone can download all the data (data mining), and ICANN requires every registry and registrar to run a Whois server.

With the split in responsibilities between registries and registrars, and the constant misuse of registration data, RFC 3663 was created to explore using LDAP instead. LDAP offered structured queries, well-known result formats, and built-in access control so registries could restrict who sees what.
sections.plainLanguage: Whois is old and messy: it gives everything to everyone in hard-to-read text. LDAP is more organized, like a real directory, and can say 'you can see this but not that.'

sections.title: Service Architecture
sections.content:
The Referral LDAP Service has three tiers. The registry server holds three Directory Information Trees: one for top-level domains (following DNS hierarchy like dc=foo,dc=com), one for name servers, and one for referrals to registrars. Each registrar server holds its own TLD tree (containing the domains it manages) and a name server and contact tree.

The third tier consists of registrant servers, which are not specified by the RFC; registrars can refer to registrant-operated LDAP servers to allow domain owners direct control over extra administrative information. This three-tier model mirrors the organizational split between registries (who manage TLDs), registrars (who manage individual registrations), and registrants (who own the domains).
sections.plainLanguage: The system has three layers: the registry (knows all .com domains), the registrar (knows which ones it sold), and the registrant (the owner themselves). Clients can jump from one layer to the next using LDAP referrals.

sections.title: Data Structure and Search Restrictions
sections.content:
Registry and registrar DITs follow the DNS domain hierarchy, with TLDs at the root, second-level domains below them, and name servers and contact information under each domain. The RFC uses standard LDAP object classes (domain, ipHost, inetOrgPerson) from existing RFCs rather than defining new ones. Entries are related algorithmically; for instance, a name server entry under a domain is named cn=nameserver1,dc=foo,dc=com.

To prevent expensive searches on a public service, the RFC strictly limits what queries are allowed. Users cannot browse all domains at the TLD level; they can only search for specific domains, perform substring searches (minimum 3 characters), or request information about known name servers. Registrar servers distinguish between anonymous access (showing only basic fields) and authenticated access (showing sensitive contact information to authorized users).
sections.plainLanguage: Data is stored in a tree like a phonebook: directories contain subdirectories. The server says 'you can look up a specific name, or search for names starting with these letters, but you cannot browse everyone.' Authenticated users see more details.

sections.title: Implementation and Lessons Learned
sections.content:
The RFC describes three types of clients built for the service: web-based, C-based, and Java-based. The web client was the most used but confused users unfamiliar with LDAP. The graphical clients proved that LDAP client libraries were adequate, but required detailed knowledge of the DIT structure to work correctly. The RFC notes that many implementation challenges were not with LDAP itself but with client usability and data normalization.

A key discovery was that normalizing data (storing name servers and contacts separately to avoid redundancy) created 115 million entries instead of 20 million, so a custom backend was needed to make the non-normalized view work without intra-server referrals. The experiment revealed that referrals (which LDAP uses to direct clients between servers) behaved inconsistently across implementations, sometimes getting stuck in loops or returning only referrals instead of data.
sections.plainLanguage: Building real clients showed that LDAP works technically, but users found it confusing. Storing the data efficiently also required custom code instead of off-the-shelf LDAP servers.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
The RFC notes that its access control demonstration (DN-based authentication with simple passwords) would not be adequate for production deployment and should not be used as a model. Real deployments would need stronger authentication and authorization. The document also mentions internationalization was not covered, as the experiment focused on ASCII domain names.

No IANA considerations apply to this RFC. The document is Experimental; it describes a research project that worked well enough to understand the challenges but remains a proof-of-concept rather than a recommended practice.
sections.plainLanguage: The security here was just a test; real systems would need much better protection. This whole approach was experimental, to learn what could work. The lessons learned might inform future directory services for domain data.
